archetype.name: Bubble Team (power-play propped)
archetype.definition: A middling Central club whose power play is hiding a 5-on-5 game that is being badly out-chanced, leaving it fighting just to stay near the playoff line.

report.headline: A .500-looking start built on the power play, not on 5-on-5 play
report.take:
Nashville is 2-2-2, sixth in the Central, and 24th of 32 on the site's Teams tab. That ranking is closer to the truth than the record. Six games is a small sample. Even so, the underlying picture is stark: the Predators own only 42.3% of the 5-on-5 expected goals (27th) and 43% of the shot attempts (29th). Their forwards and defense both grade D, and the goaltending grades C. This is a team getting pinned in its own end and scrambling to stay in games.

What keeps the standings respectable is the power play. It is converting at 27.3%, sixth in the league. The veterans running it carry most of the scoring: Steven Stamkos has 7 points, 5 of them on the power play, and Roman Josi has 4 power-play points among his 6. Across the nine listed forwards, 12 of the 30 points came on the man advantage. Goaltending has been roughly average rather than a rescue. Juuse Saros sits at a .897 save percentage and -0.2 GSAx, and the team's goalies are at 0.6 GSAx overall. The record isn't a lucky one either: Pts vs Goal Diff is a modest +0.4, and the 16-19 goal count matches a team that loses a bit more than it wins.

The numbers hide a top-heavy problem. The players logging the most minutes are being caved at even strength. Ryan O'Reilly plays nearly 22 minutes a night with a 27% xGF share and is a -5. Josi plays over 25 minutes at 27.9%, Stamkos is at 29.5%, and Jonathan Marchessault is at 30%. Meanwhile Filip Forsberg, Alexander Kerfoot, Matthew Wood and Jack Drury are all close to even. The bleeding comes from the top of the lineup, not the bottom. Defensively, opposing centers are scoring well above expectation against Nashville (26th), while wingers are held under (8th). A 97.8 PDO says some puck luck has gone against them, but no amount of shooting regression fixes a 43% Corsi.

History argues the 5-on-5 collapse is partly a small-sample exaggeration. Nashville sat around 49-51% xGF in each of the last two seasons, even in the 30-44-8 year. Expect the shot share to drift back toward the mid-to-high 40s and the power play to cool from its 27% pace. That nets out to the same territory as last season's 38-34-10: on the fringe, likely just outside, unless the top line and Josi's pair stop losing their minutes.

strengths.title: A power play that's carrying the offense
strengths.body: Nashville's 27.3% conversion ranks sixth and is doing most of the scoring work. Stamkos and Josi drive it, with 5 and 4 power-play points. It is a genuine skill: these veterans' production rests on it. Still, a 27% rate rarely holds over a full season, so expect it to slide toward the low 20s, where it lived the last few years.

strengths.title: Middle six holding even at 5-on-5
strengths.body: Away from the top minutes, the forwards are breaking even. Forsberg (49.1% xGF), Kerfoot (49.8%), Wood (49%) and Drury (47.4%) are basically trading chances, and Adam Edstrom has 3 goals in about 13 minutes a night. The depth is fine. If the coaching staff leans on these groups more at even strength, the overall shot share should recover.

strengths.title: Competent kill and average goaltending
strengths.body: The penalty kill is 12th at 84.2%, and the goalies are slightly above expected as a group. Matt Murray posted 0.8 GSAx in his one start. This is no wall, but it isn't leaking either. It gives the team a floor while the 5-on-5 play sorts itself out.

concerns.title: Getting out-chanced badly at 5-on-5
concerns.body: A 42.3% xGF share and 43% CF share are both bottom-six in the league. That's a team spending most of even strength defending. Part of it is small-sample noise: Nashville was near 49% xGF last season. But a gap this large over six games reflects real problems in puck possession. It's the single biggest reason the site ranks them 24th.

concerns.title: Top minute-eaters underwater
concerns.body: O'Reilly (27% xGF, -5), Josi (27.9%) and Stamkos (29.5%) carry the most ice time and are losing it badly at even strength. Their point totals look fine only because of the power play. If this persists, the team has no 5-on-5 driver at the top. Matchup usage, with these players facing top lines, may explain part of it, but that is still a structural issue to watch.

concerns.title: A blueline with little support behind Josi
concerns.body: The six listed defensemen have one goal between them, and Josi has most of the group's points. Nick Perbix has 0 points and a -5 in nearly 19 minutes a night. The D grade reflects a group that neither moves the puck up nor suppresses chances. Opposing centers are scoring well above expectation (26th), a sign that coverage through the middle is breaking down.

trend.note: Nashville alternated losses and wins through the first five games, including two one-goal road losses in Toronto and Ottawa. Then a 2-5 home loss to Vegas made it two straight defeats. Six games in, there is no clear direction yet, only a consistent shot-share deficit underneath.

weekAhead.headline: Two winnable home games, then a real test in Boston
weekAhead.body:
The week opens with two home games. San Jose (3-3-0, 26th on the site) is the one opponent getting out-chanced even worse than Nashville: 37.3% xGF, 31st. The Sharks also carry a D- goaltending grade and a 91.5 PDO, and wingers have scored well above expectation against them. That's the best chance all week for Forsberg and Wood to produce at even strength. St. Louis (3-2-1, 14th) is a different problem. The Blues drive play at 55.1% xGF and will test Nashville's 5-on-5 weakness directly. They do leak to centers, though, with more than half the points against them going to that position, which suits Stamkos, O'Reilly and Kerfoot.

After a long break, the week closes in Boston (5-2-0, 5th on the site). The Bruins carry A grades on the blueline and in goal and rank third in goals against. Their 107.6 PDO suggests some of that will cool, but not by next week. The opening is Boston's 76% penalty kill (22nd), which lines up directly against Nashville's best weapon. Taking three or four points from the two home games would be a realistic, good week.

keyMatchups.title: Nashville power play vs Boston's kill
keyMatchups.body: Nashville converts at 27.3%, sixth in the league, while Boston kills only 76%, 22nd. Against a team that rarely gives up goals at even strength, special teams are the Predators' most realistic path to scoring in Boston. Drawing penalties will matter more than usual.

keyMatchups.title: Blues' shot share vs Nashville's possession
keyMatchups.body: St. Louis owns 55.1% of the 5-on-5 expected goals; Nashville owns 42.3%. This is the game that will show whether Nashville's possession problem is fixable. The Blues' power play is only 14.3% (25th), so Nashville can afford to be physical without being punished much.

keyMatchups.title: Sharks' leaky goaltending and wings
keyMatchups.body: San Jose's goalies are below expected and grade D-, and opposing wingers are beating their expectation against the Sharks (27th). It's a spot where Forsberg, five assists but zero goals on 16 shots, should finally break through.

weekAhead.watch: Whether O'Reilly, Stamkos and Josi can push their 5-on-5 chance share back toward even against St. Louis, a team that out-chances most opponents.

restOfSeason.body:
Nashville's recent history is a team hovering around 49-51% of the expected goals. Six games of 42% is more likely an early dip than a new baseline, so expect the 5-on-5 numbers to recover toward the high 40s. The power play's 27% pace will probably settle lower, and the two effects roughly cancel. The 97.8 PDO should drift back toward 100, which helps a little. With D grades up front and on the blueline, the ceiling is limited. The realistic band looks like last season's 38-34-10, a bubble finish that likely lands outside the top eight in the West.

What is sustainable is the depth forwards' near-even play and a decent penalty kill. What will regress is the power-play conversion. The open question is the veterans at the top of the lineup: if their even-strength minutes stay this lopsided, the floor is closer to the 2024-25 collapse than to a playoff push.
swingFactors: Top line and Josi's pair winning their 5-on-5 minutes
How far the power play cools from 27%

confidence.note: Six games; shot-share and PP rates are far from stable this early.
